title: Fast restart + graceful degradation runbook for OOM spikes
content:
Summary:
This is a working runbook for handling short-duration OOM spikes in the serving runtime where full host replacement is overkill and we prefer a fast, deterministic restart plus graceful-degradation path to preserve external SLOs. Goal: get tenant traffic back to acceptable tail latency and error-rate quickly while avoiding cascade OOMs and noisy restarts.

When to use this runbook (trigger):
- Alert: host/hostgroup OOM spike alerts firing (pager-level) or mass OOM kmsg entries across multiple pods within ~60s.
- Symptoms: sudden tail-latency blow up, high 5xx from shims, KV cache eviction thrash, or repeated container restarts correlated to memory pressure.
- Not for: hardware failures, kernel panics, or persistent OOMs on cold-start path — escalate to full incident playbook.

Quick-impact checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Post to #sre-incident with short TL;DR: hosts affected, tenants impacted, immediate mitigation being attempted.
2) Run quick telemetry checks (PromQL snippets below) to confirm memory spike scope and whether it's single-host, per-host, or system-wide.
3) If single host or single AZ with >80% of affected pods: initiate fast restart of affected serving process and enable graceful-degradation routing for that hostgroup.
4) Monitor error-rate & latency for 5 minutes. If improvement not observed, escalate to do a host ejection and failover to spare capacity.

Telemetry quick checks (Prometheus / Grafana):
- Per-host memory spike: sum(container_memory_usage_bytes{job="kubelet", cluster="prod", pod=~"srv-.*"}) by (instance) / sum(machine_memory_bytes) by (instance)
- OOM kills: increase(rate(kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason{reason="OOMKilled"}[5m])) by (node)
- KV cache churn: rate(redwood_kv_cache_evictions_total[1m]) by (host)
- Request tail latency (p99): histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(redwood_request_duration_seconds_bucket[1m])) by (le, route))

Immediate mitigation actions (step-by-step):
1) Circuit traffic away from the host (soft-eject): patch the routing policy for the hostgroup to scale weights to 0 for ~30s so in-flight requests drain. Command: (internal) curl -X POST https://control-plane.local/api/v1/routing/hostgroups/{hg}/soft-eject -d '{"duration_s":30}'
2) On the host, attempt graceful restart of the serving process (preferred): systemctl restart redwood-serving || supervisorctl restart serving-process. This preserves node-level processes like prefetch and eviction coordinator if they are separate.
3) If process won't restart cleanly or OOMs persist, perform a fast container recycle: kubectl -n serving rollout restart deployment/srv-worker-<hostgroup> --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node-name> OR kubectl delete pod <pod> --grace-period=5 to force quick restart.
4) If multiple pods on same node fail to restart due to host-level memory exhaustion, trigger host-level evacuate + reboot: (SRE-only) run: /usr/local/bin/evacuate-node --node <node-name> --target-pool spare-pool && request host-reboot via infra runbook.

Graceful degradation knobs (temporary):
- Reduce batch size and max inflight per-worker (dynconfig tweak): POST /api/v1/dynconfig/serving -d '{"batch.max_tokens":256, "batch.max_concurrent":8}' with change-id and short TTL 30m.
- Enable degraded model variant (cpu-friendly or quantized) for critical routes: route override to model:openai/gpt-compat-quantized-v2 with fallback window 10m.
- Disable non-essential background work on host: set env REDWOOD_PREFETCH=0 in deployment, or flip flag in orchestration (quick toggle).
- Increase KV cache eviction aggressiveness for non-tenant keys: flip fv:kv.eviction.policy=aggressive (temporary) to free host memory.

Post-mortem triage checklist (after immediate stabilization):
- Collect kernel dmesg / OOM logs from node and attach: journalctl -k -b -1 and /var/log/messages.
- Capture pod-level cgroups and memory.stat for affected containers.
- Export KV cache metrics and last-seen wasm/eval traces for tenant keys.
- Correlate deploy/rollout events: check /deployments for recent rollouts in the 30m window prior to spike.
- Snapshot GC/allocator histograms if available (tcmalloc/hoard logs).

Automated remediation play (to consider for follow-up automation):
- Auto-soft-eject rule: when OOMKilled rate per node > 3 in 2m AND node memory usage > 85% then schedule soft-eject and trigger fast-restart pipeline on affected node.
- Fast-restart cold path: orchestrate a rolling restart of only serving process not host; attach circuit-breaker thresholds to avoid cascading restarts.

Communication templates (short):
- To oncall channel: "SRE alert: OOM spike on hostgroup hg-12 -> soft-ejecting 1 host, enabling degraded routing, restarting serving process. Monitoring p99 & 5xx. Will update in 10m."
- Incident summary to owners (post stabilize): include affected tenants, duration, mitigation actions, and next steps for follow-up.

Playbook commands & useful snippets:
- kubectl get pods -n serving -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node-name>
- kubectl logs -n serving <pod> --previous --tail=200
- curl -sS 'http://prometheus/api/v1/query?query=rate(kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason%7Breason%3D%22OOMKilled%22%7D%5B5m%5D)'
- curl -X POST https://control-plane.local/api/v1/routing/hostgroups/{hg}/soft-eject -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SRE_TOKEN' -d '{"duration_s":30, "reason":"oom-spike-fast-restart"}'

Known pitfalls & caveats:
- Fast restarts can surface cache warmup penalties; if routing back too aggressively we may see p99 regressions—monitor both error-rate and p99 before re-introducing traffic.
- Do not flip global dynconfig flags without short TTLs; mistakes here can affect all customers. Use per-hostgroup overrides when possible.
- If we see sequential OOMs across hosts during restarts, stop and escalate — likely a systemic config regression (memory leak in recent rollout).

Post-incident follow-ups (owners & tickets):
- INF-8123 (linked) — create a short task to add an auto-soft-eject controller prototype (owner: Priya Kapoor, due: 2025-02-01).
- GH PR #4428 — revert candidate for recent batcher memory expansion (owner: Diego Morales, in review).
- Telemetry: add a synthetic that triggers degraded route and measures end-to-end latency under fast-restart to ensure SLOs are preserved (owner: Arielle Chen).

Open questions and experiments to run: 
- Can we safely snapshot & restore a trimmed KV cache state across a fast restart to reduce warmup? (experiment owner: Diego)
- How low can we set the batch.max_concurrent in production for high-throughput tenants before throughput regression is unacceptable? Run A/B on low-traffic HGs.
- Should we implement a host-level memory reservation guard for background processes (prefetch/eviction) to prevent them from consuming headroom needed by the serving process?

Appendix: quick debugging checklist (ordered)
1) Confirm OOM kmsg and affected pod list.
2) Soft-eject host(s) if isolated; start graceful restart.
3) If restart fails: force-delete pods to get new ones scheduled off the host.
4) If host memory exhausted: evacuate node and boot spare.
5) If multiple hosts across AZs: escalate to full incident and engage infra & oncall-sre leads.

Notes to self (working):
- Add a Grafana panel showing soft-eject events timeline vs. p99 and OOMKilled count.
- Draft small automation prototype to do auto soft-eject & restart in a controlled manner (circuit-breaker enabled).
- Coordinate with product owners of large tenants before auto-rollouts that might temporarily change model variants during degradations.

This is a living doc — keep concise mitigation steps near the top and move retrospective notes to the bottom as the playbook stabilizes. Refs above and link to INF-8123 for tracking engineering work.
